chapter: The Famous Door, Billy May and the Palomar fire
title: The Palomar fire aftermath: Basie's arrangements and playing without music
summary: After the 1939 fire it was Basie, not Ellington, who sent arrangements; the band crossed the country to Boston playing from memory and head arrangements.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well, I'll tell you, Pat, why that happened. You see, after the Palomar fire in 1939, there was an erroneous rumor that got around that Duke came to our rescue and gave us a whole bunch of arrangements, you know, to get restarted, because we'd lost the whole library and everything. Actually, he didn't give us any arrangements, because I don't even think he knew about the fire or knew of our predicament. The guy that did give us some arrangements was Count Basie. Because Basie was supposed to follow us in and he was in the same boat with us. He came all the way out to California to open and there was no place to open. And he was booked in for four weeks, so his managers were in a

scramble to get him booked, and here we were with no instruments, no library, and we had jobs to go to, but it was a question of what are we going to play. Now fortunately that band had been together for so long with the same personnel, we had so many head arrangements and the guys could remember all the arrangements. We went all the way across the country, back to Boston, to the Southland Cafe, which took about a month to get there, and we never had a music stand in front of anybody the whole trip. In the meantime the arrangers were busy and -- writing the -- at first they were starting to send them. I said, "Don't send them, we're doing fine. We haven't got time to rehearse anyway. We'll get there. Just have them in Boston and then we'll do it there." So we actually played that whole trip with no music, and this gassed a lot of people. They'd look at the band, you know, and there's no music. But these guys knew everything. We had a tremendous amount of head arrangements anyway, and the same personnel, plus the fact that they were able to remember enough of a lot of the things that were written down that they could play them.
Well, I read somewhere that a lot of band leaders sent you arrangements when they heard about your predicament. Basie was the only one?
What did you do for instruments instantly?
